subsubtopic: PROPOSED INCENTIVES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In order to overcome our trade deficit of $11 billion a year in manufactured products-the ones that produce jobs-we must improve our productivity, and to do so, we must offer incentives which will persuade producers that they will be able to pay for the new plant, machinery and production systems they will have to buy in a reasonably short space of time, and in this way make it as easy as possible for them to make the usually high expenditures involved. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That the government allow all capital expenditures involved in improving productivity to be written off in one year; and second, a plant to be rewarded in the form of a cash bonus at the end of the year in direct proportion to its increase in productivity during the year.
By improving our productivity, we can lower costs and selling prices, and in this way greatly increase sales of our manufactured products.

Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that under the constitution the date of the general election is determined according to the whims of the Prime Minister; considering that this procedure is obsolete and has an effect on the national economy due to the suspense experienced by those who have an economic and financial impact, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the House direct the government to introduce in the House a bill aimed at including in the Statutes of Canada a provision stating that from January 1978 the federal general election will be held every four years at a date set under the legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The commission created by the Native Council of Canada in 1975 has recently reported its findings on the number of natives in jail. It has discovered that the major contributing factor to the disproportionate number of natives in jail is the lack of meaningful economic bases in the majority of communities from which the prisoners came. In view of the seriousness of the problem, which correlates with an unemployment rate of over 75 per cent in the native communities, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That the appropriate federal departments and agencies in consultation with the native communities meet immediately for the purpose of introducing programs to correct this serious problem.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport regarding aviation safety. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously safety is an overriding consideration. The regulations and the degree of safety implicit in them is very clear evidence of this. The point I was making, which is referred to in the correspondence from my officials at different times, is that to give inspectors the power on their own judgment to close down a service, without going through due process of law, is clearly a very strong level of power to have in the hands of any official or person, without giving a chance to appeal or to go to court before the effects of the judgment are suffered. It must be understood that what was in issue was whether our licensing inspectors who find something wrong are able to impose a penalty upon a carrier by closing that carrier down, with

Obviously there is a conflict. The conflict is weighing the matter of civil liberties against the primacy of air safety. The minister has not clarified that for me, for any member of the House, nor for the public, in particular the passengers who are using that service. Will the minister seriously consider a public inquiry into this whole matter, or at least table the document in order for us to have a look at it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

There are some very important issues in terms of civil liberties that perhaps should be looked at by a parliamentary committee. In the meantime, we have had an investigation by officials of my department. Surely hon. members opposite have to agree, because of the report furnished to the public by the Globe and Mail, that the investigation was very thorough and revealed significant problems. These significant problems related to the way the regulations were enforced, and also that there was a lack of inspectors. We moved immediately to add to the number of inspectors. We have passed the necessary regulation to transfer some power to regional directors to suspend operators' licences and the like, in order to make enforcement more effective. In other words, it is very prompt action to ensure safety will be guaranteed. On the other hand, if the civil liberty question is a problem, we will be glad to look at that further.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, December 7, consideration in committee of Bill C-l 1, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds-Mr. Chretien-Mr. Turner in the chair.

When the committee rose on Wednesday, December 7, 1977, clause 14, with amendments, was under consideration. Shall clause 14 carry?
On clause 14-Inventory allowance.

Mr. Chairman, there is a provision in the proposed bill concerning terminal loss and depreciable property. Subclause (4) of the amendment reads:
That for taxation years ending after March 31, 1977, in respect of depreciable property, a taxpayer be required to deduct a terminal loss in the year in which it arises whether or not the taxpayer has a source of income in that year.
I can see that would present difficulties to certain taxpayers, and I wonder if the minister or the parliamentary secretary- since the minister does not seem to be here-could explain the reasoning behind that clause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Chairman, before replying to the hon. member I want to apologize for the minister's absence. Unfortunately, he is stuck on the tarmac in New York, where he was speaking to some businessmen last night and this morning. We hope he will be here for this afternoon's session. However, he wants to apologize to the House for his inability to be here. I wonder if the hon. member would be kind enough to repeat his question.

My question was with respect to the amended subclause (4) of clause 14. Can the parliamentary secretary give an explanation of the subclause, because I can see a number of instances where it would be a definite hardship on the taxpayer to deduct a terminal loss, especially in a year when he had no other income.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I think we have discussed this clause. The hon. member should be aware that one of the important reasons for this clause was to move this out of the regulations and put it in the act. It was the result of representations made to the department and to the minister. That is an important change from the past.
The technical change simply transfers the terminal loss rules from the regulations to the act. This loss arises when depreciable property is disposed of for proceeds which are less than the undepreciated capital cost. The amendment also ensures that a terminal loss can be claimed by the taxpayer whether or not he still operates the business in which the assets were used. Technically, under the existing act the terminal loss after the year the business has ceased is not deductible.
Is the parliamentary secretary saying that it is simply the same provision taken out of the regulations and put into the act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. It also ensures that the terminal loss can be claimed by the taxpayer whether or not he still operates the business in which the assets were used. That is the new part of this section.
That was my next question. It now extends the right to that deduction in the event there is no income from that same business? It is an extension to that degree, is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I am not sure if this matter relates to the proper clause. I will let the Chair decide that, because I do not know where else this could fit in. A number of times the minister has said there would be reductions in federal tax because of the amendments in this bill, that people would therefore have more income, that that would help stimulate the economy, and so forth. It has come to my attention that, with the changes which have been made in provincial income tax rates, the average taxpayer will in fact have no extra income in his hands because the provincial tax will in many cases more than sop up the reductions allowed by the federal government. In support of that, instead of a provincial rate of 32.5 per cent in British Columbia, we will have a rate of 46 per cent. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can comment on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Chairman, that affects provincial taxation; it does not affect federal taxation. However, some of the changes referred to by the hon. member are because of changes in the fiscal arrangements act.

I thought I had conceded that in my preamble. Of course it is a provincial tax, but it affects the federal tax. The minister claimed credit for granting a reduction of some $200 and that taxpayers would have this money in their pockets in January and February so that they could spend it and stimulate the economy. I believe it is also a fact that the new provincial rates came about through negotiations between the provincial and federal governments. My concern is twofold. This seems to be a result of negotiations with the federal government. Furthermore, it seems to give the lie to what the minister says; that taxpayers will have extra money in their pockets. Will they, or will they not? Can we find that out? Does the federal government take any responsibility for these negotiations?

One of the most important aspects of clause 14 is the question of the inventory allowance which we discussed last time this clause was before the House. Obviously, this will have to be monitored on a regular basis to see if it has achieved the desired results with respect to economic conditions in the future.

$485 million is the best guess at the federal level? Is that the total impact of that credit, or is there also a loss of revenue at the provincial tax level on account of the investment tax credit?

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary may wish to hold this question until the minister returns. The day before yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance if he could indicate whether any consideration was being given, with respect to investment credits, to tying them to some employment condition in the sense that an investment credit would be forthcoming provided the company could show some job-creation, and also that investment credits be tied to first-decision situations. I wish to follow up on my colleague's questions concerning the 3 per cent allowance on year-end inventories. I ask the parliamentary secretary if this is not an allowance which in some measure may overcome the effects of inflation on profits. First of all, why was a fixed rate of 3 per cent of year-end balances arrived at, when inflation was obviously much higher than that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this provision was made to assist the cash flow of industry. It was a judgment call, rather than a figure of 3 per cent.

Could the parliamentary secretary tell us why some other method was not used? An arbitrary figure of 3 per cent of inventory surely affects different businesses in different ways. If, for example, a business has a large inventory and a small turnover, it would get a bigger benefit than a business with a small inventory and a large turnover. There are many other methods of accomplishing what I think the government wanted to accomplish by giving this allowance. One would obviously be by the last in, first out method.
If the attempt is really to enable businesses to match inventory costs with revenues, then surely the system of last in, first out would be more equitable, and therefore a preferable system. I am not sure that it would not be simpler, as well. Why was something like that not adopted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I indicated earlier, Mr. Chairman, many methods were discussed by officials. We looked at what other countries were doing. This method was chosen because it was very simple to implement. The LIFO method, which the hon. member refers to, is a very complicated method, and although that could still be discussed with respect to the future, in terms of alleviating the situation in the short-term it was decided to use the simpler method which would also be beneficial to both large and small corporations throughout the country.

I am not sure it is any simpler, Mr. Chairman, to try to fix the rate at 3 per cent. But if that is the case, if it was a matter of simplicity, I am surprised that the government has finally concerned itself with simplicity in income tax matters, because there has not been any simplicity or equity in the last little while. When one is attempting to match costs, the most recently purchased goods are probably what one is selling in any event. I suppose we cannot except the parliamentary secretary to change his answer; we will have to accept it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

When trying to solve some of the cash flow problems, we felt very strongly that the simpler

method would be the one most readily acceptable for small businessmen throughout Canada.

Mr. Chairman, dealing with subsection (5) of clause 14, there is some wording which I feel should have a little explanation. With respect to applications concerning companies with fiscal periods after the end of March 31, 1977, they then go into a formula that the 3 per cent inventory allowance which may be claimed is an arithmetic calculation based on 365 days. Could the parliamentary secretary indicate why this arbitrary March 31 cut-off is put in? I understand it is causing problems to people who have year-ends that are following in the short period defined here. Unfortunately, sometimes it is the smaller businesses and retailers falling into this period who are having difficulty living with the provision as it is now worded. Could the parliamentary secretary explain why we have the date March 31-beyond the obvious; it was budget night-or could we not simplify it and say January 1 and save the problem of the distinction that is obviously being made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is right when he indicates that this is a problem area. If you will allow me, I would just like to read specifically some of the reasons for the change. The original ways and means motion of March 31 indicated that the measure would only be applicable to taxation years commencing after 1976. Many representations were received pointing out that this was inequitable for those taxpayers whose fiscal periods commenced in 1976 but were substantially in 1977. In response, the scope was expanded to cover a taxation year which started in 1976, in which case the new inventory allowance would kick in on March 31, 1977. This means some companies could start receiving the inventory allowance up to three months later than other companies, but that minor imbalance would have been costly to avoid.
Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the parliamentary secretary could indicate if any consideration is being given to perhaps relieving whatever the inequity is in time for the next budget.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to discuss a matter with the parliamentary secretary. I have consulted some of his colleagues and I understand that this clause refers to replacement property under capital gains. The bill now relieves a taxpayer who makes a capital gain on the sale of a property-a farm or small business-and puts all the proceeds from that sale into a larger and better farm or small business. That person would be exempt from the capital gains tax on a first sale. However, he would be liable to pay capital gains tax if he subsequently sold the replacement property. He would be exempt from the capital gains tax on the first sale, but would be liable if he sold the second or replacement property.
I have specific cases in mind-there are probably a dozen other cases in my constituency of farmers and small businessmen who sold a property two, three or four years ago and used all the proceeds to purchase a more economic farm unit or small business enterprise. They were liable for the capital gains tax even though they used all the proceeds from the sale, plus additional borrowings, to acquire a more economic enterprise. I appreciate the fact that the bill makes provision to exempt such people from capital gains tax on the first sale, and that this provision came into effect on March 31, 1977. Could the parliamentary secretary tell me if he and his officials would sympathetically consider and act upon this suggestion right away, or perhaps we could stand the clause for 20 minutes while an amendment is drafted to make this retroactive or deemed to have been in place when the capital gains tax came into force.
I appreciate that the officials would need a few minutes to assess what such refunds would cost. I do not want to be misunderstood: I am fully in agreement with the principle of capital gains tax. I agree with Mr. Carter who said "A buck is a buck.". In the case I give as an example a small farmer who sold two small farm units and realized a capital gain of $8,000 in each case, so is liable for $3,500 capital gains tax. He used the proceeds to acquire a larger farm so that he and his son would have a unit large enough that they could farm together. The problem is that this took place prior to March 31, 1977. Therefore, I appeal to the parliamentary secretary to see if the wording of the clause cannot be changed. Perhaps a limitation of so much money or so many acres could be inserted. I would agree to that. Those who do not need the benefit should not get it.
Has the parliamentary secretary had time to consult his officials and come up with some fast wording that would allow a capital gain on the sale of property where the proceeds of the sale are used to buy another property in all such cases in the last three or four years. I am sure it would not involve too many cases. I would limit my request to small farmers and businessmen who are not out to make a capital gain but who want a more economic unit. I sense, from conversations with members on all sides, that there is some support for this idea.

It may involve $500,000 or $1 million in refunds, but surely that is a small amount to set against a fair application of the principle of capital gains tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member understands that in any tax issue there is always the question of retroactivity. Nobody is totally satisfied when the government introduces changes. Obviously, we are very sympathetic to the hon. member's representation. I have made representations along the same lines on behalf of my constituents. Where would we draw the line, however? This could be an administrative nightmare. There would be reams and reams of work. Why pick on this particular tax change to be retroactive, and not some other area?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into a long argument with my colleague. I know he agrees with me in principle, but I wish he would not obfuscate or run in back alleys with the matter. Obviously, the line would be drawn at a purely replacement sale. Where a person has bought and sold half a dozen farms in the last four years, exemption should not be considered. Such person is obviously out to make a capital gain without paying taxes, so I would not exempt this kind of transaction. Where there is a legitimate instance of replacement for the economic well-being of a small farm or small business, that is where I think retroactivity should apply.
Since the capital gains tax is relatively new, it is not as though it would be necessary to go back 100 years or even ten: at the most, it would involve five years. There should be no administrative nightmare either, because as I see it there would be no exemption or refund unless the taxpayer made application. It would be a relatively simple matter for the department to review the tax returns for the previous four or five years, and if they were satisfied that the capital gain on the original sale was totally reinvested in replacement property, an exemption or, if necessary, a refund could be made. At most, a few hundred or a few thousand cases would come to the department's attention, and surely they could handle that.
It seems to me, the way the bill reads, that in the area of replacement property there is sufficient limitation to eliminate people who have turned property over four, five or even ten times in the last five years. Obviously, such people are not trying to improve their farm or small business and should not be eligible for refund of capital gains tax on the first sale.
I appreciate that since the minister is not here, another minister might have to move an amendment to the bill on his behalf; but I appeal to the parliamentary secretary to give us better reasons than we have heard for not doing it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the principle number of retroactivity which the hon. member suggests were applied, this would indeed be discriminatory. He is forgetting about all the small businesses in the country to which this clause also applies. Thus there are tens of thousands of files to be investigated, and this is an administrative nightmare.

Why wouldn't they apply?
December 9, 1977

One of the principle reasons the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is under some misapprehension and I think the parliamentary secretary is at cross-purposes in answering him-is that if they went back to the Income Tax, and saw what section 44 was dealing with, it is exactly the deferral of gain on involuntary dispositions.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has been talking about the example of an individual who had sold or exchanged properties three or four times in a row. That is not an involuntary disposition. If we look at the involuntary dispositions that are considered in clause 44, we can go either to clause 13 or to clause 54 where the definitions of the dispositions envisaged by this particular clause are considered. These are, first of all, compensation for property unlawfully taken. That is compensation under an insurance policy for property that has been stolen and which by reason of inflation there has been, shall we say, an increase in value. Or there could be instances where land may have been unlawfully taken and compensation has been made to the rightful owner.
Second, I refer to the case where property has been destroyed, whether real or personal property. In the case of a house which was built or acquired 20 years ago, and this year is destroyed by fire, then of course the insurance value will be much greater than the acquired value.
Lastly, the one I am concerned with is where there has been expropriation. These are the rules that might apply, and there is a change in the whole of clause 44.
I say, Mr. Chairman, we would have had less refinement and amendment over the years if the government had heeded the advice and the action taken by the opposition at the time of the income tax changes in 1971. I then proposed, on behalf of the official opposition, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, who was then the financial critic of the New Democratic Party-at least, he supported me up to a point- that all farm lands sold or disposed of, or passed to heirs, which would continue in bona fide agricultural purposes would not be subject to capital gains, period. If that motion had been accepted, we would not have all these refinements. However, we have had some refinements since that time.
The then minister of finance, Mr. Benson, refused to accept that farm lands should not be subject to capital gains. Then there was the first amendment-if there was a legitimate passage from father to son, or from father to daughter-either by sale or by death-but it had to be in the immediate family: it could not be sold to a neighbour who was carrying on farming. Of course, it did not apply to family incorporated farms, which was absolute nonsense-bureaucratic nonsense. It still is, if I may say so.
In many parts of the country farmers have been encouraged to incorporate their farms for a number of valid reasons. When there has to be disposition of an incorporated farm, immediately the capital gains guillotine falls on them. This is wrong. As a matter of fact, we would not have a good number of these refinements with regard to farm land if there had been a total exemption provided the lands continued for bona fide agricultural purposes. I think the House would generally agree to
Income Tax
that. But no, there has been this absolute insistence by the government that farm lands, unless they are exempt-even if they are going to be sold and continued as farms-will be subject to capital gains.
I notice that in this clause the effective date, where there has been an expropriation action, is deemed to be the date of the judgment of the lawsuit. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that is wrong because there is a great deal of difference between the date of a lawsuit and the date the funds payable under the lawsuit become available to the affected landowner, who then has to go about to effect changes in property as envisaged under the act. In this connection I quote from page 28 of the bill which refers to the day on which the taxpayer's compensation for the property is finally determined by such tribunals or courts. That should be the day on which the compensation is paid following the determination by such a tribunal or courts.
In the case of the government of Canada-I think everyone here will agree-by the time the judgment of the Department of Justice traced through to the department affected-say it is an expropriation by the Department of Transport-the Department of Transport will have a demand on the Department of Supply and Services to issue a cheque. This can take not only weeks but months.
If there is any recalcitrances as I saw in the parks department following the decision concerning perpetual leases, it could take years before the department will acknowledge it was wrong and that it must accede to the decision of the tribunal. Here, again, is a complication following capital gains on farm land. I advise the minister, if I could have his ear, that capital gains tax as such brings in very little, relative to the administrative complexities not only of the Department of National Revenue taxation officials but also the ordinary citizen.
Having recourse to tax consultants, whether they be accountants or lawyers, from a national point of view is much ado about nothing. The mountain of labour is tremendous. There is a bureaucratic mountain on one hand and the public mountain on the other. The result of that joint labour is but a puny mouse. It is not worth a candle in this country at the present time.
Capital gains is nonsense. It is much more of a nonsense where it affects farm lands that are going to be destined for bona fide agriculture.
This tax came about as a result of claims that land developers were making great amounts of money and not paying taxes. Any lawyer worth his salt knows that in so far as income is concerned under the Income Tax Act, that is any income arising out of a venture. The purchase of a parcel of land for the purpose of subdivision or otherwise, other than for bona fide farm purposes by a farmer or one who intends to farm, is known as a venture. There are judgments galore in the Supreme Court of Canada which determine that the profit on such a venture shall be income and therefore subject to income tax.

There are those who want to be demagogic about property development, academics who could not find their way out of a paper bag when it comes to tax matters. Others give a cosmetic appearance about doing something about a particular problem that has been already covered. There are those who motivate on both sides who travail on these mountains.
I am sure the Minister of Finance would be the first to admit that the yield on capital gain, bearing in mind the action of the stock market and the value variations in other fields, has produced little tangible revenue. However, the pages in the Income Tax Act have been expanded inordinately. First, they set up the capital gains tax. Second, they set up and describe the exceptions. Those exceptions take pages and pages and pages. Precious few people understand them. The minister, like myself, is one who cannot understand them because the complexity is so great.
There is one value of a tax system which the minister and his officials always forget. In order for a tax system or a tax law to be just, it must be readily understood. That is fundamental to any tax system. If anyone in this country, barring a very limited number of people, understands the workings and ramifications of the Income Tax Act, whether they apply to individuals or corporations, I have sadly missed my guess.
In 1971 the government introduced legislation, Section 44 as it then stood. Now it is all being replaced. Why? Because there are some hard cases under it. If hard cases make bad law, then bad law makes hard cases. In so far as this act is concerned, most of the capital gains legislation and the exceptions thereto are bad law because they make hard cases. One should look at this amendment in the context of what I have said. I hope that some day we will be able to excise a great deal out of the Income Tax Act.
Income tax reform basically would be the simplification of income tax. Every time one seeks an exception or an exemption of a particular kind, the act is complicated. The return is complicated and the act and the tax are less understood. From the public's point of view, this is an extreme loss.
1 hope we can get a full confirmation from the minister of what he wants to do other than tinkering with this section which, frankly, 1 do not think should be in the act. Capital gains on farm land for farm purposes should not be there.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the hon. member for Edmonton West. He was about as helpful as the parliamentary secretary. Some of the points he made had nothing to do with the point I raised. I was talking about voluntary sales, for example where a farmer sells a three quarter section farm to buy a one and one half section farm so that he has an economic unit.
I agree that in the case of an expropriation, an involuntary sale where the Department of Highways pays him "X" number of dollars for his farm, there is a capital gain. My point is this: if he spends all the proceeds of that voluntary or involuntary sale on replacement property, will he be exempt from capital gains tax, and only liable to capital gains if he sells the replacement property?

I am not interested in exempting the doctor or lawyer who buys a farm every three or four years as a hobby. That is not his prime occupation. That person should be liable for a capital gains tax.
The hon. member for Edmonton West was accurate when he said we supported his contention in 1972 to exempt bona fide farmers or storekeepers if that was their only livelihood. However, we are not interested in exempting a doctor or lawyer, who has a piece of land as a hobby, from capital gains tax. He should not be exempted if he only uses land to horse around on or make a few extra bucks. I am not talking about that kind of case.
The hon. member said we are just complicating the act. I am more interested in it being fair, with the good principle of a capital gains tax being applied in a good manner. The provisions in clause 18 give effect to what I am proposing. If this is a good principle in the bill to be effective March 31, 1977, why is it not a good principle effective March 31, 1972, or 1973, whenever the capital gains took effect? It is equally valid. I do not think it would be impossible from an administrative point of view. The onus would be on the taxpayer to prove that all the proceeds from a sale went into the purchase of replacement property. If he could not do that, he should be liable for capital gains tax.
I am asking that the principle of clause 18 be taken to apply as far back as the date upon which the capital gains tax was put into effect. In a case where a farmer or a small businessman was obliged to pay capital gains tax in such circumstances he would be eligible for a refund. I hope the minister's officials have been able to devise an appropriate amendment to give effect to what I have requested.

I should like to tell the Minister of Finance that when I made inquiries about this particular matter I received an excellent letter from the Minister of National Revenue in which he said:
Section 18 of Bill C-l 1 proposes an amendment to the Income Tax Act dealing with the reinvestment of proceeds of disposition of a former business property in a replacement property. If the taxpayer so elects, the gain from the disposition of the former property would be the lesser of:
(1)	the gain therefrom otherwise determined, and
(2)	the excess of the proceeds of disposition of the former property over the cost to him of the replacement property.
I agree with that interpretation. I also agree with the intent of the amendment. I am asking the minister this: would he not agree that the good principle being applied to the capital gains provision in this case might not just as validly be applied retroactively to the bona fide farmer or small businessman who uses all the proceeds from the sale of his property to invest in a replacement property so as to continue his primary, if not his only, means of livelihood? The Minister of National Revenue told me that unfortunately for my constituent this amendment took effect only as of March 31 last. Surely it would be a relatively simple matter to deem this benefit to apply some three to five years earlier than that date. I ask the minister to reconsider his policy and not to allow the matter to be complicated by side issues such as were raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: For the third time, Mr. Chairman, I have to tell the hon. member that we have listened to his representation but we have no intention of changing the date.

The minister has told us that if the change is of an involuntary nature involving a third party the term is two years, and if it is voluntary the term is one year. In the first case the person concerned has some control over whether he should make a disposition. I am interested in what happens when the government cannot make up its mind on certain issues with the result that a period of time goes by, as happened, for instance, in the case cited by the hon. member for Edmonton West. Does the two-year limit run from the time the court decision is made?
It seems to me we have not corrected anything here. Insurance companies will not make a decision within the two years if they are engaged in lengthy litigation, and there likely will be lengthy litigation because this is an involuntary disposition resulting from, say, expropriation by government, fire or theft. I do not see the purpose of the two year limit.
I agree with the minister that there is some sense in a one year limit, because then it is voluntary. There is control over it. In that case there is a rollover. But in the second case I do not think there is a rollover. It is not voluntary. The rollover is caused by extraneous considerations, something over which a company has no control. If a company is half way through litigation and it gets an offer, it will have to take the offer as being within the two year period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think so. According to the act, section 44(2), the situation is quite clear. Paragraph (a) reads "the taxpayer has agreed to an amount as full compensation to him for the property lost, destroyed, taken or sold". If the taxpayer does not agree, later on in the act section 44(2)(b) provides that the day is "the day on which the taxpayer's compensation for the property is finally determined by such tribunals or courts". This means that if the taxpayer does not agree, the time starts to run once the court has made a determination or the taxpayer agrees to a settlement.

Paragraph (c) reads "where a claim . .. has not been taken before a tribunal or court of competent jurisdiction within two years of the loss... the day that is two years following the day of the loss" will be the deciding date. My point is that in the first case a rollover is made on a voluntary basis. In the second case where a third party is involved, if the taxpayer goes through the courts he will have two years following the court's determination. In many cases the taxpayer does not want to take the matter to court, but he is under a compulsion to do so.
Every day I handle compensation cases which are 10 or 12 years old. People have been waiting for the company concerned or the compensation board to do something for them. I am sure many members of parliament are sitting back waiting for their automobile insurance companies to do something for them. We wait for other people to take action. If a person is

December 9, 1977
Income Tax
not in the wrong, then why the hell should he go to court? We are not talking about a voluntary action but something a person is forced into.
The hon. member for Edmonton West, who was trying to help the minister out, referred to a case where a considerable period of time elapsed following an expropriation and the government never got around to making out the cheque.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, if I heard the hon. member correctly he is completely misinformed. He said that I was trying to help out the minister. My point was that the provision in this act is wrong. It provides that the period of two years shall run from the date of the order of the tribunal. To me, the date should be the date of payment of the cheque. Oftentimes government departments take months and months to pay money to the intended property owner. I was not trying to help out the minister; I was criticizing the proposed amendment.

May I thank the hon. member. In my roundabout way that is the point I was trying to make. The two years was at the discretion of the department, or the courts, or somebody other than the person concerned. If the hon. member for Edmonton West was arguing the other side of the coin, I apologize for having misunderstood. I understood him to say that the delay in issuing the cheque was not the fault of the individual.
I appeal to the minister that this is a field where we could be more flexible. It seems to me that in so many fields today we are asking Canadians to defend themselves against government, whether it be in connection with unemployment insurance, compensation, expropriation, damages or income tax. I have had dozens of people write to me in connection with income tax problems they experienced last year. This silly department is now sending out unpleasant letters to everyone, informing them that it is time to start making payments and to fill in their 1977 tax forms. If I do not pay my income tax because the government is at fault, why should I have to pay interest on the money that I have not paid? After all, the government has made the mistake.
The roll over which takes place from a smaller operation to a bigger operation is only a portion of the business operation, the same as the purchase of a tractor, a combine or any piece of machinery. No restrictions should apply to that once in a lifetime, or once in an every-20-years proposition. Businesses are pleased to deal with capital gains because their capital losses can be written off. As far as the rollover in the agricultural field is concerned, that person is not talking about losses. He had those losses before making the transfer. He will not roll over that proposition and replace his present farm with a new farm in order to take a loss. There will be an expenditure involved, and it will take some time for him to pay back the money borrowed.
The point in time that should be considered is when a person receives insurance money for his property being destroyed, and

not two years hence, or at the conclusion of litigation. I should point out that a buck is a buck is a buck. A single farm operation cannot be put into the same category as the individual who turns over 50 farm properties a year. In both instances capital gains tax must be paid, but it should only be paid when the moneys are received.
People in the London and Chatham area are finding it impossible to acquire replacement land for one reason or another. Thus they travel to northern Ontario in order to look around. There is a vast difference between the type of farming in northern Ontario and that of southern Ontario. Prices are being exaggerated and accelerated because of this. These people require time because the farming structure is different, the season is different, and the types of crops are different. If these people are in receipt of money from the first proposition, it is mandatory for them to invest it within one or two years. They are faced with the possibility of not finding property in northern Ontario which is within their price or borrowing range. This is not a voluntary situation because they have been forced out due to the fact that no land is available in their area. They are hemmed in and boxed in thus they have to sell.
If hon. members give consideration to this section, they will be opposed to passing it as it is structured. Also they will oppose it because of the way Section 44 has operated over the last three or four years in relation to capital gains. I will vote against this because I think it should be turned down.

It is a principle that I find, from talking with hon. members on all sides, meets with agreement. I do not understand the reluctance of the minister to extend a good provision in clause 18 back to the implementation of the capital gains tax. There is no justification for not doing so.
The other points raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Edmonton West are only partially in tune with the point I raise. Surely the minister is correct in saying that this provision should apply right across the board. All I am saying is: let us apply it right across the board back to the time when the capital gains tax came into effect. I plead with the minister again. There is no substantial reason for not agreeing to do that.

that Bill C-212, to provide for the establishment of the office of Parliament Hill Curator, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services.

Bill C-212 provides for the establishment of the office of Parliament Hill Curator. I came to think about such a bill because of an incident which occurred in the House last year or two years ago when I sought information from those people responsible for removing the glass windows in the House when
[The Deputy Chairman.]
it became necessary to replace them by these beautiful coloured windows we can see now around the House. The removal of those leaded windows was done quite simply-they used a sledge hammer to smash them off and not a single piece of those historic windows was salvaged. I am sure that museums and numerous other historical associations in the country would have been quite interested in keeping some of those window panes but none were saved.

For instance the episode when these windows were removed with a sledge hammer and replaced by the present beautiful coloured windows representing the floral emblems of all our provinces and territories was as close to a sacrilegious incident as you can come in the House of Commons. Every museum in the country would have treasured an item from this Chamber. This is one incident of many which have occurred here resulting from the fact that there is no one in charge of ensuring architectural integrity, that the furniture, the works of art, the sculptures in wood and stone are preserved or conserved in a way the people of Canada would expect them to be safeguarded.
Over the years furniture belonging to historic Canadian figures has either been sold, disappeared, or simply thrown away. Furniture of this kind is probably around Ottawa and would be worthy of a place in any museum if it could be found. It would certainly be appropriate for the refurbishing going on in the East Block. It has disappeared because there is no one individual who has taken it upon himself to keep an eye on these antiques.
During the refurbishing of the House of Commons this past summer I came in one day and discovered that under this carpet there was a teak wood floor of great value, which had been left during all the demolition period not covered-not even plywood or plastic over it. The workmen were just throwing things from the ceiling on to the floor. Some day an architect may come along and say in the interests of esthetics that the carpet should be removed and this beautiful floor exposed. Whether or not that happens, I simply make the point that no one is checking on all this. I feel strongly that because that is the case-

-because there have been many mistakes made here, either by Public Works or by Parliament staff, a member of the staff of the House should be entrusted with the necessary responsibilities to supervise.

I would hope that this person who would be appointed as curator for Parliament Hill would be able to advise the people responsible both in Ottawa and Hull as to what action they may or may not take with respect to all these items.
There have been a number of instances during the last few years where gradually the Parliament Hill panorama has been cut off from a large percentage of the people living in the Ottawa-Hull area. The view of the Peace Tower and Parliament Buildings has been obliterated by the skyscrapers which

December 9, 1977

have gone up in central Ottawa. The same thing is now happening on the Hull side. It is too late now to do anything about that. Before it is impossible for anyone in the surrounding area or anyone approaching Ottawa to see the Parliament Buildings and Peace Tower from afar, we should move to arrest further deterioration of this view. It means a lot to most Canadians.
I feel that the post of parliamentary curator would carry with it an obligation to advise and use whatever avenues are available to encourage the authorities who have responsibility for the height of buildings in the vicinity of Parliament Hill to use their discretion and prevent a further downgrading of the importance of Parliament Hill.
I do not feel that the wording of this bill is sacrosanct. It can probably be improved substantially. Frankly, what I would like to see is the subject matter of the bill referred to a committee.
I understand it would normally be referred to a committee dealing with members' services. If so, I would be prepared to accept that. I hope the subject matter will be referred to that committee. If it meets with the consent of members of the House, I would ask one of my colleagues to move that the subject matter of Bill C-212 be referred to the committee dealing with members' services.

Mr. Speaker, I rise very briefly to congratulate-
Parliament Hill Curator

-the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) for his bill, an outstanding bill indeed, and I want to commend him for his interest in Parliament Hill.

I do not want to hold up the bill. It should go to the committee.
From time to time I have been concerned about changes that occur in this building. There does not seem to be any consultative process. Occasionally things that are historic, traditional, and meaningful, disappear. The most recent instance struck me a few weeks ago when I was showing visitors from the constituency through the Parliament Buildings. As I approached the Railway Committee Room, I stated that the room was full of tradition and history and that it contained some marvellous paintings. As I opened the door, there were no more paintings. Entirely without notice or indication, they had somehow been moved. I do not know where they are. I would be interested in finding out whether they can again be displayed somewhere in the building.
The Railway Committee Room was turned into a sort of boudoir by some interior decorator who was allowed to run tame, using every stale cliche in the interior decorator's trade. That room has lost its history, tradition, and significance. It had impressed many people. It had many functions.
When the bill goes to the committee, I hope we can have some explanation of what happened, particularly with regard to the vast painting of the Fathers of Confederation. I know it features fine old Conservatives such as Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Georges Etienne Cartier. It had a place of honour. That place seems to have disappeared along with the excellent painting of the Vimy Ridge Memorial. That haunting picture has also vanished from the scene.
We very much need someone who cares to take care of and be concerned about the decisions that are made in this place, particularly when something may well be lost if someone who is sensitive to the nation's history is not in a position of some authority.

If the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) did not have my support before he made his speech, he certainly got it when

I had the privilege not long ago of visiting Washington where the planners had free rein in preserving the so-called vista. The net result was to preserve a series of obsolescent buildings within view. It created a slum within the heart of the city.
I remember visiting that city in 1970 with other members of this House, including the hon. member who sits opposite, an old friend and former Speaker of this House, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). We did a tour of the dome. I am sure he can remember 1970. Every shop, every place of business had been burned by arsonists. They looted the centre part of that capital city. It was spoiled by misguided policies which prevented the erection of new buildings and drove all new offices out into the periphery. Thank heavens we have not repeated those errors in this city. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PRESERVE ARTIFACTS FOR POSTERITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) on his Bill C-212 for the establishment of the office of Parliament Hill Curator.
I am convinced that the aim of this bill is quite laudable, according to the remarks made by hon. members who have taken the floor on this issue. I remember that some three or four years ago maybe, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had raised before this House the issue of building construction in the vicinity of Parliament Hill, skyscrapers whose impact on visitors who come to the Hill is that they hide from them the sight of Parliament and tend to make visitors and Canadians alike forgetful that they stand before Parliament or if you want the Parliament Hill of the National

Capital of Canada, since, when arriving in Ottawa, which is after all the nation's capital, one would expect the Parliament buildings to espouse a predominent perspective in their own immediate surroundings.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert had at that time received the support of all parties represented in this House and the National Capital Commission was given a mandate with very limited powers to protect this environment and make representations to the authorities of the city of Ottawa, and also on the Quebec side to the city of Hull, so as to ask them not to engage in or make any progress toward the construction of skyscrapers.
Unfortunately, and I do not know exactly for what reason, the National Capital Commission has not been able to make its view prevail since year after year we notice that this trend continues unabated. And now we realize it is a little late to act, as the hon. member for Laprairie just said when he gave explanations on Bill C-212. In my opinion, starting from now, I think that we should take all the means at our disposal to preserve this surrounding.
The purpose of the bill is to preserve all that can be preserved from an historical point of view, and I am in favour of this bill. It should be passed as quickly as possible, precisely to stop other valuable things from disappearing for one reason or another.
Mr. Speaker, the motion just introduced by the hon. member who preceded me to have this subject matter referred to an ad hoc committee is quite rational. But the committee will have to consider the matter very seriously within the spirit of the bill. That committee will then have to report to the House and the House will then have to take the means to bring about the results sought under Bill C-212. Otherwise it would be a waste of time, nothing would get done and in five or ten years there will still be members around to regret here in this House the fact that we did not think far enough to protect things we should be proud to leave to the generations after us.
So I think this is a very serious matter, a matter of national pride and real, genuine nationalism, and I am convinced that if we go at the bottom of things we will be able to do something very practical and that in years to come this will give results. So the administrators who will come after us will continue in the same way and we will be able to preserve as much as possible what can be preserved.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PRESERVE ARTIFACTS FOR POSTERITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to add a few words to this debate. I have been here so short a time that I come with a fresh approach to these wonderful buildings and this highly cherished part of our national life.
I would like to see an advisory group established by the curators of our museums. It could perhaps be called the Friends of Parliament Hill. People in communities across the country might wish to loan things to the parliament buildings so that they could be shown to the whole country.
December 9, 1977

I have often wondered why our committee rooms do not have things hanging in them. I find those rooms just a little sad and I wish that, say, in the Parliamentary Restaurant, we could see some of the wonderful pictures which I know are in storage. We do not have a national gallery as yet and perhaps this place could be made even more beautiful if there was a committee which could plan to display these things in our wonderful buildings.
One of the things I could not get over last summer, as we sat here in July, was that when I went out in the evenings for a walk I would find whole families standing just outside the doors. They came from all across the country. If you asked them where they came from they would often ask about these wonderful buildings. I think there should be far more going on here in the summertime when families come to reach out and see their parliament buildings. There are public servants in this city-I think of those in Public Works and in the National Capital Commission-who dearly love this building and who have cared for it over the years. I do not think they get the support either from public opinion or from within the parliament buildings themselves to stage events out on that wonderful lawn in the summertime in order that the people who come here from across the country could see or do more right on the Hill.
Perhaps because I am a local member I see many classes of children coming here in the spring and at Christmas time. I tell them a little about parliament, and I know the security service here is wonderful about conducting tours for them. Children, when they return to schools, are often asked to write essays about their visit here and are asked to tell about what they saw.
I wish we had the kind of brochures I have seen given out at Queen's Park. They tell a little of the history of that place and some anecdotes about it. I think if we had a curator or someone who really cared about it perhaps he would turn out to be not only safeguarding our heritage but one who would be something of a marketer who would tell about this wonderful place.
Every time I take round a school group I always show them Vimy Ridge stone. To me, this was the first great national event in our history when we became a nation. Only recently did I hear the wonderful story about the masonic plate which fell down in the fire, how they found it, and it is now hanging outside the Library. These are all real stories concerning the history of this place. Whatever happens to the bill, I hope my hon. friend will think of it not only in terms of safeguarding our past but of telling our story to the Canadian people.

Parliament Hill Curator
The Commission on Parliamentary Accommodation, composed of members from both Houses of Parliament, dealt with other possible facilities for housing members and staff. It dealt not just with the chambers here but with other buildings where we work. I recommend that when this matter goes to committee and is studied with some care and in some depth, reference should be made to some of the material in the hands of one of the deputy ministers of public works seconded to Mr. Justice Abbott's staff, Dr. James Langford. There is a lot of good material there which would be invaluable in assisting the hon. member for Laprairie, his aims and objectives.
I am not going to take up time because I believe that private member's bills, if they are good, should go to committee. I do not intend to talk out this bill, as was the case last week when we were debating a bill having to do with by-elections in Canada. The amount of time before a by-election can be called in Canada is the longest of any western democracy. Liberal members, including the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) in particular, decided they did not want to follow the democratic practice of representing the people, people who remain unrepresented because of the death or resignation of their member, and talked out a bill which would have required that a by-election be called earlier. I hope this bill goes to committee and I wish it the best of luck as I resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, I join with other members in supporting the hon. member's bill. Judging from the opportunities I have had to visit other legislatures around the world, we have in Ottawa one of the finest examples of a parliamentary facility. Anything we can do to enhance this facility, especially to tell Canadians about it, is very worth while.
I hope that as this information is organized and prepared, not only will it be made available in book form but as a film, film strips or slides so that students, not only in Ottawa but across the country, can see for themselves how the Parliament of Canada-the House of Commons, the Senate, and the Governor General-functions.
Yesterday I attended a luncheon for Dr. Vogel from the Federal Republic of Germany, who was presented with a new book on the Parliament of Canada. I had not had an opportunity to see the book before but it really is an excellent document and I hope all members have the opportunity to see it. It would make an excellent document to present on formal occasions.
80027-42V2

December 9, 1977
Parliament Hill Curator
As this committee studies the subject matter of the bill before us, I hope that someone, perhaps under the auspices of the chairman of that committee, will consider the advisability not only of documenting the information about our wonderful parliament buildings but providing the information in a popular, readable form for student groups.
I should like a short film running for about 15 minutes to be prepared for the use of student groups. Then when student groups visit us here, or when we go to high schools in our ridings, we can show them parliament in action-something it is difficult to summarize in a short space of time. For example, we often get off on one aspect of parliament, such as constituency work, committee work or the question period, and as a result I do not think the students get an over-all view. This sort of information should be made available to members for use with students and school groups. We should also have a short written summary of the functions of the Parliament of Canada.
I will not take up any more time of the House. I support the bringing forward of this important topic in the House this afternoon, and I am sure that the standing committee which will consider this bill will come up with many worth-while suggestions as a result of its study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I support this bill and I am not going to talk it out. I just want to make a comment or two, prompted by my hon. friend from Ottawa-Carleton who talked about Canadian paintings. I should like to see more of these in the parliament buildings and in other buildings on the Hill. Members of parliament, not only ministers, should be given the privilege of hanging Canadian paintings on their walls. We have an abundance of such paintings hidden away in buildings in Ottawa.
When talking about the Parliamentary Restaurant recently some of my colleagues asked me about the big long hall which leads to the parliamentary restaurant. Some of my colleagues in Quebec have asked me why, since we have pictures of Prime Ministers of Great Britain, a country for which I have great affection since it gave us our British parliamentary traditions, which I support as one of the best of parliamentary systems, we do not hang pictures of prime ministers of France, since we believe in the two founding nations. I disagreed with them entirely. I do not want to create friction with anybody, but I think that when we have this museum in the new East Block we might transfer these paintings of Prime Ministers of Great Britain to the East Block, and this will relieve me of the pressure of explaining the presence of foreign prime ministers.
I should like to recommend the establishment of the office of Parliament Hill curator. I am sure the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) will join with me in my effort. Visitors to parliament hill have different ethnic backgrounds, and they should be able to see the creations of Canadian artists adorning the corridors. There is a richness in Canadian paintings because of the multicultural background of this nation.
